== Biography ==

Alice is a young girl of clear mind and steady observation, making her way through the bewildering landscape of Wonderland with a curious mixture of caution and practicality. She is inclined toward watchfulness, taking time to observe before drawing conclusions. When she came upon the three gardeners engaged in the curious business of painting white roses red, she drew near to watch them at their work, and when she at last spoke, she asked their reason with careful timidity.

Though her manner is often quiet and her words measured, Alice possesses neither timidity nor indecision when the occasion calls for assertion. At the tea party, when the March Hare and Hatter cried out "No room!" at her approach, she contradicted them plainly, declaring with decided indignation that there was plenty of room, and seated herself in a large arm-chair at the table's end as though the matter were settled. Her education is evident in her knowledge and the quiet pride she takes in it. She had read about courts of justice in books and was quite pleased to discover that she knew the names of nearly everything there. The word "jurors" she turned over in her mind several times, being rather proud of knowing its meaning—for very few little girls of her age possessed such knowledge.

Alice observes the creatures and people around her with attention, and draws her own conclusions from what she witnesses. Finding the Duchess in an affectionate temper, she was glad of it, and reflected that perhaps the pepper which had made her so savage at their earlier meeting in the kitchen was the cause of her former unkindness. Alice's own thoughts sometimes wander into fancy: when walking with the Duchess, she found herself imagining what sort of Duchess she might make, and promising herself that her kitchen should contain no pepper at all.

Her progress through these impossible events is carried out with a kind of wondering practicality. She speaks carefully, especially when in doubt, sometimes checking her words before they are fully spoken. Yet she ventures remarks and asks questions, and listens to the strange answers Wonderland provides, accepting the dream-logic around her without complaint.

== Narrative role ==

Alice is a young girl whose extraordinary journey begins when she chases a White Rabbit with a watch down a rabbit-hole out of curiosity, tumbling through a deep well filled with floating cupboards, bookshelves, and pictures. During her lengthy fall, she observes an empty marmalade jar while contemplating mathematics and geography. Finding herself alone in this strange realm, Alice feels profoundly lonely and wishes to see her pet cat again. She encounters a Mouse who promises to tell its sad history, though the creature grows angry when she misunderstands it.

Alice is mistaken for the White Rabbit's housemaid and agrees to retrieve his missing items from his house, only to become trapped in a small room with her arms and legs extending out the window and chimney. She subsequently enters the Duchess's kitchen, which is filled with smoke and chaos from excessive pepper. At an afternoon tea party, Alice finds herself among the March Hare, the Hatter, and the Dormouse, though they cry out "No room!" when she arrives. She responds indignantly that there is plenty of room and sits down in a large arm-chair at one end of the table. Offered wine by the March Hare, Alice is subjected to the endless illogical banter of her companions, which frustrates her greatly—she leaves the tea party in anger and disgust.

In the garden, Alice observes three gardeners busily painting white roses red in an effort to hide a planting error before the Queen discovers it. She approaches them and asks with timid politeness why they are painting the roses. One gardener explains that they fear the Queen will have them all beheaded if she finds a white rose-tree where a red one ought to be. When the Queen's magnificent procession arrives, Alice deliberately refuses to bow, displaying unusual courage for her position. In a bold act, she saves the gardeners from the Queen's soldiers by concealing them inside a flower pot. She later discusses her discomfort with the Queen's cruelty with the Cheshire Cat, finding unexpected companionship with that peculiar creature.

Alice returns to the croquet game where the Queen sentences numerous players to execution. The Gryphon tells her that the Queen's threats are empty and that no one actually dies. The Duchess becomes obsessed with finding moral lessons in everything, testing Alice's patience with relentless philosophizing. When the creatures demand Alice recite a poem, she mangles it into "The voice of the Lobster" instead of the expected verse about the sluggard.

Alice arrives at the trial of the Knave of Hearts, accused of stealing the Queen's tarts. Though she has never been in a court of justice before, she has read about them in books and is quite pleased to find that she knows the name of nearly everything there. She observes the King wearing both a crown and a wig as he serves as judge, and watches as twelve creatures—animals and birds—write their names on slates as jurors. She takes pride in this knowledge, reflecting that very few little girls of her age knew the meaning of "jury" at all. As the trial reaches its climax, Alice grows to full size and declares the court to be nothing but a pack of cards. In the commotion that follows, she accidentally upsets the jury-box with her skirt while standing up, tumbling the jurymen to the crowd below.

== Personality ==

Alice is defined by her insatiable curiosity. When she encounters the gardeners painting white roses red, she finds it "a very curious thing" and draws near to watch them closely, eager to understand what she observes. This same quality extends to her observations of the world around her: she has read about courts of justice and takes genuine pride in recognizing the formal machinery—the judge, the jury-box—pleased to discover that she "knew the name of nearly everything there."

She possesses a firm sense of self-respect and will defend it readily. When the creatures at the tea party cry "No room!" she responds with indignation, declaring "There's plenty of room!" and sitting down with conviction. The same spirit appears when confronted with circumstances she finds unjust or absurd: she does not passively accept what she is told, but questions and resists when she judges resistance warranted.

Yet Alice is not reckless in her speech. When the Mock Turtle prompts her about eating lobster, she begins to speak of her own experience but checks herself hastily, recognizing that her claim might be questioned or misunderstood. This pattern of restraint—thinking before speaking—suggests she weighs her words carefully, even in moments of impulse.

Alice reveals a reflective nature in her treatment of others. Upon encountering the Duchess, she considers that the creature's earlier harshness might have been caused by the pepper in the kitchen, a charitable interpretation that assumes temporary circumstance rather than fixed temperament. She engages earnestly with questions of morality and meaning, venturing tentative disagreements—suggesting that perhaps not all events contain a hidden lesson—without hostility or defiance, as if reasoning through ideas rather than arguing.

== Relationships ==

'''[[Gryphon]]''' — acquaintance. Alice converses with the Gryphon during her time in Wonderland.

'''[[Cheshire Cat]]''' — friend. Alice introduces the Cheshire Cat to the King, calling it her friend and asking permission to present it.

'''[[White Rabbit]]''' — acquaintance. Alice encounters the White Rabbit at the trial of the Knave of Hearts, where he maintains order in the court.

'''[[King]]''' — acquaintance. The King addresses Alice at the trial, approaching her with curiosity about the Cheshire Cat she has befriended.

'''[[Mock Turtle]]''' — acquaintance. Alice listens to the Mock Turtle and converses with him, discussing her lack of familiarity with the sea and its creatures.

== Trivia ==

* Alice had devoted time to reading about the procedures of courts of justice, and discovered her bookish knowledge most useful in the courtroom of the King and Queen of Hearts, where she could name the judge by his wig and identify the jury-box by its arrangement.
* She took great pride in her understanding of the word "jurors," repeating it aloud to herself, being rather pleased to know it when very few little girls of her age possessed such learning.
* Alice had never dwelt beneath the sea, nor had she ever tasted or made the acquaintance of a lobster.
